output.title: Designing against positioning drift starts with one anchor
output.body:
If you want to design against positioning drift, start with one bounded workflow decision: what is the one customer problem or outcome your business says it consistently solves? That is the positioning anchor. Everything else can be checked against it.

For a small business, the useful question is not whether you can write better copy. It is whether your current workflow keeps sending mixed signals. Pick one repeatable place where drift shows up: how you triage customer inquiries, how you answer sales questions, or how you negotiate project scope. Choose the one that most often creates confusion.

Then write the anchor in plain English and use it as a manual check in that workflow for a short period. If the same questions keep coming up, or if scope keeps expanding in ways that pull you off-message, you have found a real control point. If the workflow stays consistent, the anchor is probably doing its job.

AI can help later by reinforcing that wording inside documents, email, CRM, or back-office workflows, but only after the owner has confirmed the anchor is actually right. That is a support tool, not a decision-maker. A small bit of discipline goes a long way.

Which workflow in your business surfaces positioning ambiguity most often? Start there, because it is usually the cheapest place to test the anchor first.
